Standard or extended parental leave: compare the household cash calendar

Five graphics separate published gross EI parameters from net leave income, work return dates, changing costs and the cash needed over an equal window.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare level-income parental-leave budgets over the same 78 weeks

Interactive planning lab

Standard-plan cash after the common 78 weeks$19,400
Extended-plan cash after the common 78 weeks-$440
Extended plan: additional starting cash needed$6,640

One fixed program-parameter graphic is separate from the editable cash scenarios. This is a single-parent EI planning illustration outside Quebec, not eligibility, benefit-amount or employment-leave advice. The default 35/61 weeks reflect published one-parent maxima, not shared-family maxima or guaranteed entitlement. Parent net leave income is entered independently, potentially including a separately verified employer top-up; published gross percentages are not applied to net pay. The selected leave weeks have level net income and leave spending; work income and work spending begin the following week, with no simultaneous leave payment in the model. Other household income stays fixed. The common 78-week window begins at the first modeled parental week, not a statutory deadline. Setup occurs at time zero; bills precede week-end income. No maternity weeks, waiting/receipt lag, sharing, QPIP, Working While on Claim, tax calculation, changing top-up, childcare subsidy, inflation or job guarantee is calculated. Negative cash is an unmet need, not approved borrowing.

The central idea

Compare the same period of household life. Benefit receipts alone omit work income, different spending phases and the money needed before later pay arrives.

01

Keep published EI rules separate from net budget inputs

The Government of Canada’s parental-benefit overview lists basic replacement rates of 55% for standard and 33% for extended benefits, subject to weekly caps and eligibility. One parent can receive up to thirty-five standard or sixty-one extended parental-benefit weeks; shared-family maxima differ.

The first graphic presents those gross percentages. It does not apply them to the work-pay control. The benefit-amount page explains that insurable earnings and other details determine the actual amount, and that some employers offer top-ups.

This is a single-parent cash illustration outside Quebec, excluding maternity weeks and benefit sharing. Confirm option rules before payments begin: the government restricts switching once a parental-benefit payment has been made. The tool neither chooses an option nor tests entitlement.

02

Compare equal time, including the work period after leave

Both alternatives run for seventy-eight weeks from the first modeled parental week. That is a comparison window, not a statutory claim deadline or the date of birth. The parent returns to modeled work income immediately after the selected leave weeks.

The standard example has CAD 600 of level net weekly leave income for thirty-five weeks, followed by CAD 1,000 of net work income. Extended leave uses CAD 360 for sixty-one weeks, then the same CAD 1,000 work income.

Other household net income is CAD 400 every week. These are independent assumptions, potentially including separately checked top-ups in the parent’s leave amount. No gross-to-net conversion, changing top-up, delayed first receipt, Working While on Claim or job guarantee is calculated.

03

Allow spending to change when work resumes

The household spends CAD 900 a week during leave and CAD 1,100 after work resumes. The higher working budget can represent an independently estimated combination of care, commuting and other changes; it is not a child-care subsidy calculation.

During standard leave, weekly income is CAD 1,000 including other household income, giving a CAD 100 surplus. During extended leave, the corresponding total is CAD 760, leaving a CAD 140 weekly shortfall. After work resumes, both cases have a CAD 300 weekly surplus under the selected budget.

Setup cash outflow is CAD 2,000 at time zero, and both cases begin with CAD 5,000. Bills leave at the start of each week; income arrives at week-end. A real partial week or different pay calendar needs a more detailed schedule.

04

Reconcile leave income, work income and spending

After all seventy-eight weeks and the final income receipts, standard-plan cash is CAD 19,400 and extended-plan cash is negative CAD 440. The CAD 19,840 difference is not explained by comparing weekly benefits alone.

Extended leave produces CAD 960 more net leave-period income in this example, but CAD 26,000 less net work income inside the common window. It also spends CAD 5,200 less because more weeks use the lower leave budget. The waterfall reconciles those three differences.

Starting cash, setup and other household income are identical, so they cancel from that comparison. The model does not assign a financial value to family time, wellbeing, career effects or preferences. Those remain part of the broader decision.

05

Measure the cash bridge before the first returning-work pay

Extended-plan cash reaches negative CAD 6,640 after week-sixty-two bills, before the first modeled work income. The schedule needs CAD 11,640 of starting cash, or CAD 6,640 beyond the selected reserve. Later work receipts do not erase that earlier need.

The cash lines show pre-income points, while headline ending cash includes the last week-end receipt. Negative balances are unfunded needs, not approved borrowing. If actual top-ups stop partway through leave or costs arrive on different dates, replace the level phases with a dated plan.

The matrix varies leave spending and other household income for the extended scenario. Work spending, the parent’s net-income assumptions and selected weeks remain fixed. Use it to test cash capacity alongside confirmed program and employer information, rather than treating a modeled result as an EI award or a recommendation about family leave.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first graphic shows published basic EI replacement percentages. All income and cash graphics use separate hypothetical net-income assumptions; no benefit award or eligibility calculation is performed. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for basic replacement percentages, one-parent week maxima, separate Quebec arrangements and option-choice restrictions. The cash window is not a statutory eligibility period; no shared or maternity benefit is calculated.

  2. Government of Canada · EI maternity and parental benefits: Amounts ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for insurable-earnings and employer top-up context. The tool applies no weekly dollar cap or benefit formula to its independent net-income assumptions, and determines no award, tax or eligibility.
